description: Voluntary, involuntary and cardiac muscle, and the location and role of the major skeletal muscles.
content_html:
Three Types of Muscle

The body contains three distinct types of muscle tissue, and understanding how they differ explains why the heart never tires, why you cannot choose to stop digesting food, and why a trained sprinter can consciously contract the quadriceps with explosive force. Each muscle type has a structure suited to its role.

Voluntary (skeletal) muscle is attached to bones via tendons and is under your conscious control. You decide to kick a football, and the voluntary muscles of your leg contract to do it. Skeletal muscle is striated — it appears striped under a microscope because of the alternating light and dark bands of the protein filaments that generate force. Voluntary muscles fatigue over time and need rest to recover. All 12 muscles you need to know for this specification are voluntary muscles.

Involuntary (smooth) muscle is found in the walls of blood vessels, the digestive tract and other hollow organs. It is not under conscious control — it contracts automatically in response to signals from the autonomic nervous system and hormones. Its contractions are slower and sustained. In sport, the involuntary muscle in the walls of arterioles controls vasoconstriction and vasodilation to redirect blood to working muscles during exercise.

Cardiac muscle forms the walls of the heart. Like smooth muscle it is involuntary; like skeletal muscle it is striated. It is unique because it contracts rhythmically and automatically (intrinsic rhythmicity) without needing external nerve signals, though the autonomic nervous system can speed it up or slow it down. Cardiac muscle is highly resistant to fatigue — it must beat approximately 100,000 times per day for a lifetime without resting. Its cells are interconnected so that electrical signals spread instantly across the whole heart wall, producing a coordinated, powerful contraction.

Key Fact

Three muscle types: voluntary (skeletal) — attached to bones, conscious control, produces joint movement; involuntary (smooth) — blood vessel walls, automatic, controls blood distribution; cardiac — heart wall, involuntary but striated, never fatigues, maintains circulation throughout exercise.

The 12 Major Voluntary Muscles

You need to know the location and sporting function of twelve skeletal muscles. Work through them from the upper body downwards.

The deltoid caps the shoulder. It is the prime mover for arm abduction (raising the arm sideways), as seen when a swimmer pulls the arm out to the side in a butterfly stroke or when a basketball player passes overhead. The biceps (front of the upper arm) flexes the elbow and supinates the forearm — essential in every pulling movement in sport, from rowing to rock climbing. The triceps (back of the upper arm) extends the elbow — it drives the arm-straightening phase of a push-up, a javelin throw and a handball shot.

The pectoralis major lies across the front of the chest. It adducts and medially rotates the humerus, generating the sweeping arm movement in butterfly swimming and the chest-pass in basketball. The latissimus dorsi (“lats”) spans the back from the lower spine to the humerus. It extends and adducts the arm — responsible for the powerful downward pull in swimming and the pulling phase in rowing. The external obliques run diagonally down the sides of the abdomen and rotate the trunk, crucial for throwing, striking and changing direction at speed.

The hip flexors (including the iliopsoas group) flex the hip joint, swinging the thigh forward in every running stride. The gluteus maximus extends the hip — it is the largest muscle in the body and drives the backward push of each stride, the power phase of a squat and the jump in volleyball.

The quadriceps (four muscles at the front of the thigh) extend the knee. They straighten the leg in kicking, jumping and the final push of a sprint. The hamstrings (three muscles at the back of the thigh) flex the knee and assist hip extension. They decelerate the swinging leg in sprinting and are among the most commonly strained muscles in sport.

The gastrocnemius is the large calf muscle that crosses both the knee and ankle joints. It plantar-flexes the ankle — pointing the foot downward in a sprint start or ballet rise. It also assists knee flexion. The tibialis anterior runs down the front of the shin and dorsi-flexes the ankle, lifting the toes during the swing phase of running and ensuring the heel strikes the ground cleanly.

Key Fact

The 12 major muscles you must know: deltoid (shoulder abduction), biceps (elbow flexion), triceps (elbow extension), pectoralis major (arm adduction/rotation), latissimus dorsi (arm extension/adduction), external obliques (trunk rotation), hip flexors (hip flexion), gluteus maximus (hip extension), quadriceps (knee extension), hamstrings (knee flexion/hip extension), gastrocnemius (plantar-flexion), tibialis anterior (dorsi-flexion).

Both cardiac and smooth muscle are involuntary, but they are structurally different. Cardiac muscle is striated (like skeletal muscle) because it contains the same overlapping actin-myosin filament arrangement needed to generate high force quickly. Smooth muscle is non-striated — its filaments are arranged in a less regular pattern, producing slower, more sustained contractions appropriate for maintaining blood vessel tone and moving food through the gut. In the exam, if asked to state one difference between cardiac and smooth muscle, the key answer is: cardiac is striated and contracts with high force; smooth is non-striated and contracts more slowly.

Taking a football kick as an example: the hip flexors contract to swing the thigh forward (hip flexion at the ball-and-socket hip joint). As the foot approaches the ball, the quadriceps contract powerfully to extend the knee (hinge joint), while the gastrocnemius plantar-flexes the ankle to point the foot for contact. The tibialis anterior relaxes to allow plantar-flexion. At the same time, the external obliques rotate the trunk to add rotational power. The bones of the leg — femur, tibia, fibula — act as levers, amplifying the force generated by each muscle. This is the musculo-skeletal system in action: muscles provide force; bones provide the rigid lever; joints provide the pivot points.
exam_tip_html: Questions that ask you to ‘state the location and role’ of a muscle expect both pieces of information — location alone, or action alone, will only score one mark of two. Use precise anatomical language: ‘the quadriceps are located at the front of the thigh and extend the knee joint’ is a full two-mark answer. On 3-mark Explain questions linking muscle to movement, use the structure: muscle name → contraction type → joint action → sporting example. On 6-mark Assess questions about the musculo-skeletal system, refer to at least three named muscles and link each to a specific movement in a named sport to demonstrate application.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Three muscle types: voluntary (skeletal) — conscious control, produces joint movement; involuntary (smooth) — blood vessel walls, automatic; cardiac — heart wall, involuntary but striated, never fatigues.
  • The 12 major muscles span the body from the deltoid at the shoulder to the tibialis anterior at the shin — each has a named location and a specific joint action relevant to sport.
  • The muscular and skeletal systems work together: muscles generate force, bones transmit it as levers, and joints provide the pivot points for movement in physical activity.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following correctly describes the role of cardiac muscle?
A) Under conscious control; attached to bones to produce movement
B) Found in blood vessel walls; controls vasoconstriction
C) Forms the heart wall; contracts involuntarily and rhythmically
D) Attaches to tendons; produces flexion and extension at joints
practice_questions.marks: C) Forms the heart wall; contracts involuntarily and rhythmically [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Identify the muscle responsible for extending the knee and state which sport action this enables.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: quadriceps extend the knee — accept any valid sporting example such as kicking a ball, jumping, sprinting, cycling. No mark if only the sport action is given without the muscle name.

practice_questions.text: Describe the location and role of the latissimus dorsi in a swimming stroke.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for location: the large, broad muscle of the back, running from the lower spine/pelvis to the humerus. 1 mark for role: extends and adducts the humerus. 1 mark for sporting application: produces the powerful downward and backward pull of the arm through the water in freestyle/backstroke, propelling the body forward.

practice_questions.text: Explain how the deltoid and pectoralis major work together in a basketball chest pass, referring to the joint movements each muscle produces.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for deltoid: at the shoulder (ball-and-socket joint), the deltoid initially abducts the arm outward to receive the ball / can assist with horizontal flexion. 1 mark for pectoralis major: adducts and medially rotates the humerus, driving the arms forward to push the ball. 1 mark for linked explanation: the two muscles work in sequence — deltoid controls the arm position; pectoralis major generates the forward push that propels the ball.

practice_questions.text: A strength-and-conditioning coach is designing a lower-body training programme for a sprinter. Assess the relative importance of the gluteus maximus, quadriceps and hamstrings to sprint performance, and justify which one the coach should prioritise.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6): Correctly identifies and describes the role of all three muscles in sprinting. Makes a supported comparative argument. Reaches a clear, justified conclusion on prioritisation. Example: gluteus maximus extends the hip, generating the rearward push that drives each stride forward; quadriceps extend the knee in the propulsive phase; hamstrings flex the knee to recover the leg and assist hip extension but are the most commonly strained muscle in sprinting. Concludes e.g. 'The gluteus maximus should be prioritised as it generates the largest propulsive force, though hamstring injury prevention is also critical.' Sustained sporting application.
Secure (3-4): Correctly identifies at least two muscles with mostly accurate roles. Some comparative argument. Partial conclusion.
Developing (2): Identifies muscles but roles are limited or vague. Little comparison.
Emerging (1): Names one muscle with a basic point.

practice_questions.text:
The table below shows the muscle cross-sectional area (CSA) in cm² of three athletes before and after a 12-week resistance training programme.

Athlete | CSA before | CSA after
Lee     | 42         | 49
Marcus  | 38         | 47
Patrice | 45         | 52

Calculate the percentage increase in CSA for Lee.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for correct working: (49 - 42) / 42 × 100. 1 mark for correct answer with units: 16.67% (accept 16.7% or 17%). No mark if percentage sign is missing.

flashcard_questions.q: What are the three types of muscle in the body?
What makes cardiac muscle unique compared to the other two types?
flashcard_questions.a: It is involuntary yet striated and never fatigues.

flashcard_questions.q: Where is the deltoid located and what movement does it produce?
flashcard_questions.a: Caps the shoulder — abducts the arm.

flashcard_questions.q: What action does the latissimus dorsi produce and in which sport is it key?
flashcard_questions.a: Extends and adducts the humerus — key in rowing and swimming.

flashcard_questions.q: Which muscle extends the knee, and where is it located?
Which muscle flexes the knee and assists hip extension?
What is the role of the gluteus maximus in running?
flashcard_questions.a: Extends the hip, driving the leg backward to propel the body forward.
Tibialis anterior — front of the lower leg.

flashcard_questions.q: What role do the hip flexors play in running?
flashcard_questions.a: Flex the hip to swing the thigh forward with each stride.

flashcard_questions.q: What controls vasoconstriction and vasodilation in blood vessel walls?
flashcard_questions.a: Involuntary (smooth) muscle in the vessel walls.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the pectoralis major's role in a swimming butterfly stroke?
flashcard_questions.a: Adducts and medially rotates the humerus for the sweeping arm pull.

flashcard_questions.q: Which muscle extends the elbow in a push-up?
flashcard_questions.a: Triceps — back of the upper arm.

glossary_terms.definition: Muscle attached to the skeleton, under conscious control, that produces joint movement during physical activity.
Muscle found in the walls of hollow organs such as blood vessels and the digestive tract, not under conscious control.
The specialised involuntary muscle that forms the walls of the heart, contracting rhythmically and continuously throughout life.
Narrowing of blood vessels, reducing blood flow through them.
Widening of blood vessels, increasing blood flow through them.
The triangular muscle covering the shoulder, responsible for abducting the arm away from the body.
The large fan-shaped muscle of the chest that adducts and medially rotates the arm.
The broad, flat muscle of the back that extends, adducts and medially rotates the humerus, producing the pulling-down arm action.
Muscles at the front of the hip joint that flex the hip, bringing the thigh forward.
The large muscle of the buttock, the primary extensor of the hip joint, producing the powerful drive backward in running, cycling and jumping.
The group of four muscles at the front of the thigh that extend the knee joint.
The group of three muscles at the back of the thigh that flex the knee and extend the hip.
The large calf muscle that plantar-flexes the ankle, pushing the foot downward.
The muscle running down the front of the lower leg that dorsi-flexes the ankle, lifting the foot upward.
